record.paper_title: Ductile-to-brittle transition and yielding in soft amorphous materials: perspectives and open questions
record.context_brief: microscopic definition and precursors of DBT
record.original_question: How should brittle versus ductile yielding be quantitatively defined at mesoscopic and microscopic scales in soft amorphous materials, and can static or dynamical precursors at those scales be connected to the ductile-to-brittle transition and the later failure scenario?

evidence.quote: One key outcome of the discussions that took place at the Lorentz Center is that the DBT needs to be defined more quantitatively . To this aim, one should first systematically look for any signature of the DBT at the microscopic or mesoscopic scale, and/or try to identify static or dynamical precursors for the DBT. In that context, the goal would be to answer the following questions: How can one define brittlevs. ductile behavior at the mesoscale and/or at the microscale? Can we connect the nature of the precursors to the DBT and the subsequent failure scenario?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a soft amorphous material (e.g., a dense colloidal suspension, emulsion, foam, gel, or molecular/metallic glass) subjected to a quasi-static or slowly-driven mechanical loading protocol (such as uniform shear at a small constant rate). Macroscopically, two qualitatively different yielding scenarios are observed: (i) a "ductile" response, in which the material flows in a smooth, spatially homogeneous manner past a yield strain, and (ii) a "brittle" response, in which yielding occurs through an abrupt stress drop associated with a localized failure (e.g., a shear band or crack). The crossover between these two regimes as a function of preparation history, sample age, or loading conditions is referred to as the ductile-to-brittle transition (DBT).

Provide quantitative definitions of "brittle" versus "ductile" yielding at:
(a) the mesoscopic scale, in terms of statistical observables of plastic activity (e.g., spatial correlations, size distributions, and clustering of local plastic rearrangements or "shear transformation zones") prior to and at yielding; and
(b) the microscopic scale, in terms of particle-level structural or dynamical observables (e.g., non-affine displacement fields, local elastic moduli, soft-mode participation, vibrational density of states, locally favored structures, or relaxation-time distributions).

Using these definitions, determine whether one can identify static structural precursors and/or dynamical precursors at the mesoscale or microscale that:
(1) appear before the macroscopic stress peak,
(2) distinguish samples that will yield in a brittle manner from those that will yield ductilely, and
(3) can be quantitatively connected, via an explicit indicator or order parameter, both to the location of the DBT in the relevant phase diagram and to the subsequent failure pattern (e.g., the location, orientation, and width of the eventual shear band or crack).
artifact.status_search_result: The question is posed as one of the open challenges identified at a 2023 Lorentz Center workshop on yielding in soft amorphous materials. Recent literature (2023–2025) on elastoplastic models, atomistic glasses, and colloidal experiments offers partial insight—mesoscale precursors such as avalanche-size statistics, divergence of a correlation length, and microscale indicators like soft spots, local yield stress, and machine-learned "softness"—but no consensus quantitative definition of brittle vs. ductile yielding at the micro/meso scale has been established, and a general predictive link between precursors and the DBT/failure scenario remains open.
